title: Renewal resetting of quantum dynamics: a classification for complete resets, a reduction for jump channels, and critical time scales
shortTitle: When randomly reset quantum systems settle down
oneLine: A quantum system reset at independent random times settles, for every gate and reset state, exactly when resets surely recur and are not locked to a lattice, even if the mean time between resets is infinite; imperfect resets reduce to complete ones under a checkable condition, and at the critical power-law hazard settling can take more than a billion steps.
abstract: A quantum system evolves step by step and is occasionally reset; the times between resets are independent and may have an infinite mean. When does the averaged state settle down, and to what? Wald, Yao, Platini, Hooley and Carollo (Quantum, 2025) inferred from estimates and numerics that, for reset hazards γ/(n+1)^α, a steady state is expected for α < 1 and probably for α = 1, but not for α > 1; this paper proves rigorously what they inferred and identifies the limit. For complete resets in finite dimension, every waiting-time law is classified: the state converges for every gate and reset state exactly when resets surely recur and their times are not locked to a lattice, and the limit or surviving oscillation is identified in every other case, including defective clocks and distinct initial states. This part is a short consequence of classical renewal theory (Erdős–Feller–Pollard, Feller, Orey). For proper infinite-mean clocks and unitary dynamics on a separable Hilbert space, the trace-norm distance to the surviving pure-point orbit tends exactly to 1 − m_pp, the reset state's continuous spectral mass, and no trace-norm convergent subsequence exists unless that mass is zero. For imperfect resets described by a general jump channel that need not commute with the free evolution, the dynamics is asymptotically complete resetting to an effective state under a unit-circle nonresonance condition (W); (W) is characterised, decidable exactly for finitely supported clocks, open and dense, and extended to conserved observables. This is a sufficient condition, not a classification of all jump processes. For the critical hazard γ/(n+1), coherences decay like t^(−min{γ, 1−γ}) with an explicit uniform remainder, endpoint and near-resonance crossovers are described, small consecutive changes are shown not to certify proximity to the limit, no rate holds uniformly over clocks, and dephasing can require more than 10⁹ steps. Exact and floating-point finite computations corroborate the formulas and examples; they do not prove the limit theorems. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Complete resets in finite dimension: every renewal clock falls into one of four regimes; a clock makes every finite-dimensional unitary reset system converge if and only if it is proper and aperiodic, and every aperiodic infinite-mean clock gives the dephased state D_U(ρ). This is a short consequence of classical renewal theory (Theorems 2.1–2.2, 4.1, Propositions 4.2–4.3, proof).

Power hazard of Wald et al.: for r_n = γ/(n+1)^α with 0 < γ < 1, the state converges to a survival-weighted mixture for α < 1, to D_U(ρ) for α = 1, and for α > 1 approaches a rotating orbit that converges if and only if the reset state commutes with the gate (Corollary 2.3, proof).

Infinite dimension: for a proper infinite-mean clock and a unitary on a separable Hilbert space, the trace-norm distance to the surviving pure-point orbit tends to 1 − m_pp; a trace-norm convergent subsequence exists only if m_pp = 1 (Theorem 6.1, proof).

Jump channels: under the nonresonance condition (W), imperfect resetting with a possibly noncommuting jump channel is asymptotically complete resetting to an effective state ρ_eff in laboratory time; (W) is characterised at w = 1, for unital and unitary pairs, is open and dense, is decided exactly for finitely supported clocks, and extends to conserved observables. Sufficient but not necessary (Proposition 5.6 gives a counterexample to necessity); examples show what each hypothesis does (Theorems 5.1, 5.8, Proposition 5.3, Lemma 5.4, Propositions 5.5–5.7, proof).

Critical clock r_n = γ/(n+1): coherences decay like t^(−min{γ,1−γ}) with an explicit remainder uniform in γ; endpoint and near-resonance crossovers; consecutive increments are much smaller than the distance to the limit for γ > 1/2; no rate holds uniformly over clocks (Theorems 7.1, 7.5, 7.6, 8.1, Proposition 7.4, proof).
Time scales: from the two-term asymptotics, coherence at z = −1 stays below 1% only after about 6.4 × 10³ steps at γ = 1/2 and about 2.3 × 10⁹ steps at γ = 0.2 or 0.8 (Table 4, numerical estimates).

narration: When reset quantum systems settle down. An Evidence Press briefing. Picture a quantum device that applies the same operation, step after step, but now and then wipes the system back to a fixed starting state, at random times. Does the average state eventually settle down, and if so, to what? Resetting is a common way to steer quantum devices, so the answer matters. In 2025, Wald, Yao, Platini, Hooley and Carollo studied rules in which the chance of a reset falls as time passes since the last one, at a rate set by a number called alpha. From estimates and simulations, they inferred the answer. This paper proves it. There are three findings. First, for complete resets, the paper covers every possible reset clock. In a finite system, the state always settles exactly when resets surely keep coming and are not locked to a regular rhythm. This holds even when the average wait between resets is infinite. For their family: with alpha below one, the state settles to a weighted mixture. With alpha equal to one, it settles to a dephased state. Above one, it keeps rotating, unless the reset state and the operation commute. Second, for imperfect resets, the paper gives a sufficient condition, not a full classification. If a checkable condition rules out locked phases, the system behaves in the long run like a perfect reset to an effective state. Finally, at alpha equal to one, settling can be extremely slow. Numerical estimates suggest over a billion steps in some cases, far beyond today's hardware. There are limits. The core mathematics is classical renewal theory, from Erdős, Feller and Pollard, Orey, and Blackwell. Finite computer checks support the formulas but do not prove the limit theorems. This is an anonymous, unrefereed candidate. So far it has had only AI-assisted checks, including an adversarial review. It has not been peer reviewed, independently reproduced or formally verified. Its paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

decisionObject.description: Long-time behaviour of the ensemble-averaged state of discrete-time quantum dynamics under renewal resetting: a classification for complete resets with every waiting-time law in finite dimension, the trace-norm defect 1 − m_pp in separable infinite dimension, a laboratory-time reduction for noncommuting jump channels under condition (W), and uniform rates, crossovers and time scales for the critical hazard γ/(n+1) studied by Wald et al. (2025).
decisionObject.scope: Independent identically distributed waiting times independent of the quantum state; fixed reset state or jump channel; time-homogeneous free evolution; averaged density matrix only. The jump-channel result is sufficient, not necessary; a characterisation of the jump processes for which the reduction holds ((W) is not necessary), a rate for the jump-channel reduction under a Sibuya clock, general infinite-dimensional channels, two-time correlations and measurement-triggered or correlated clocks are open. The time-scale table is numerical.

semanticBridge.description: Wald et al. pose no formal open problem; their hedged expectations for α > 1, α < 1 and α = 1 are quoted from their Section 4, their reset convention (a reset occupies its step and applies no gate) is the one used here, and their difference condition (Eqs. (34)–(36) of the published version) is evaluated in Remark 2.4.
remainingRisks: The paper proves what Wald et al. inferred; it does not settle a problem they posed.

The scalar and finite-dimensional complete-reset classification is a short consequence of classical renewal theory; the novelty claim rests on the trace-norm defect, the jump-channel reduction and the uniform critical-clock estimates.
